questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three problems that motivate moving from argparse to Hydra for research code?
options: Configs grow nested across model, optimizer, and data settings
Every run needs its exact resolved config saved for reproducibility
Researchers want to swap a whole group of settings without retyping every flag
argparse cannot be installed via pip
questions.explain: argparse is a standard library module and installs fine. The real motivations are nested config structure, the need to persist exact run configs, and swapping entire config groups at once.

questions.q: In a Hydra config.yaml's defaults list, what does an entry like '- model: resnet' do?
options: It deletes the model config group
It loads configs/model/resnet.yaml and merges it into the composed config under cfg.model
It renames the model to 'resnet' as a string
It has no effect unless passed on the command line
questions.explain: Entries in the defaults list select which file from a config group (e.g. configs/model/) gets composed into the final DictConfig, here making cfg.model equal to the contents of resnet.yaml.

questions.q: Given the command `python train.py model=vit optimizer.lr=0.01`, what does Hydra do?
options: It raises an error because two overrides cannot be combined
It swaps the entire model config group to the vit variant and overrides a single nested key, optimizer.lr, to 0.01
It only applies the last override listed
It ignores both and uses the defaults
questions.explain: Hydra command-line overrides can swap whole config groups (model=vit) and override individual nested keys (optimizer.lr=0.01) in the same invocation, with no code changes required.

questions.q: What does adding -m (multirun) to a Hydra command accomplish?
options: It runs the script faster using multiple threads
It launches one run for every combination of the comma-separated override values given, e.g. 3 learning rates times 3 seeds = 9 runs
It merges two separate config files into one
It disables logging for that run
questions.explain: Multirun sweeps the Cartesian product of comma-separated values across the given overrides, launching a separate run per combination, each in its own output subdirectory under multirun/.

questions.q: Why does Hydra's practice of writing the fully resolved config to a per-run output directory matter for research reproducibility?
options: It is required for the code to run at all
It makes the script execute faster
It answers 'what config produced this number' with no ambiguity, since the exact resolved values are saved alongside every run's results
It replaces the need for version control entirely
questions.explain: Because every override, default, and composed value is written into a timestamped config snapshot per run, you can always trace a reported result back to the exact configuration that generated it.
